p1.key: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalized electrons. A describes ionic bonding and D covalent bonding.
Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and a sea of delocalized electrons.

The graph rises from Na to a maximum at Si and then drops sharply: this is melting point. Metallic bonding strengthens Na → Al, Si is a covalent network, and P, S, Cl and Ar are simple molecules. Electronegativity rises steadily; atomic radius falls.

Metallic bonding is a lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalized electrons: sodium. Graphite has delocalized electrons but is covalent (no positive ions); NaCl is ionic; sulfur is molecular.
Metals consist of a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalized electrons; these mobile electrons carry the current. The cations are fixed in place.
Aluminium is a metal, even when molten: conduction is by the delocalized electrons. (Molten ionic compounds conduct by mobile ions, but Al is not ionic.)
A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalized electrons. B describes ionic bonding, A a covalent bond and D a dative bond.
Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalized electrons. A describes ionic bonding, B covalent bonding and D a coordinate bond.
Metallic bonding is strongest with small cations and a high charge density. All four have 1+ ions, and Li+ is the smallest, so the delocalized electrons attract it most strongly.

Metallic bond strength increases with cation charge and decreases with size. Al3+ has the highest charge and is small, and Al contributes 3 delocalized electrons per atom, so its metallic bonding is strongest.

Metallic bond strength comes from the attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons. A large charge (more delocalized electrons) and a small ionic radius (higher charge density) give the strongest attraction.
Metallic bonding is the attraction between cations and delocalized electrons. A larger cation charge (more delocalized electrons) and a smaller ionic radius (higher charge density) make it stronger.
